Part 1: The model

[top model] shipped this week, alongside Mythos 5.2. Anthropic says the two are the same underlying model, and [top model] is the one with broad availability. For marketing work, [top model] is the one you'll use.

Three things in the launch post matter to a marketer. Here's the first:

### 01. The price

The launch post says it plainly: [top model] generates outputs up to 30% faster than [previous top model], and it costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

What does that mean in marketing terms? A million input tokens is roughly 750,000 words of reading. A million output tokens is roughly 750,000 words of writing, thinking included. A landing page is maybe 1,000 words. So the writing itself is never the expensive part.

The expensive part is everything around it: the model reading your competitor pages, your brand guide and your previous campaigns, every subagent reading them again, and the thinking it does before each reply. That's where a bill grows, and that's what Part 4 is about.

There is also a fast mode at $16 and $80 per million tokens. For a campaign you review once, you don't need it. Keep it for a live session where you wait on every reply.

### 02. The effort setting

This is the one most people miss.

Look at the first underline: Medium effort is the default in Claude apps and Claude Code. If you open the Claude app today and paste a campaign brief, you are running [top model] at medium. You never chose it. It was chosen for you.

Now the second underline. In Anthropic's early testing on a coding evaluation, [top model] at high effort scored about level with [advanced model] at max effort, for roughly half the cost per task.

That's a coding test, not a marketing one, so don't read it as "high effort writes better ads". Read it as what it says: the effort setting moves both quality and cost, and the default is not the setting Anthropic recommends for long unattended work. We'll come back to which one to use in Part 4.

The levels, from the prompting guide, in plain words:

  • Low: quick back-and-forth and high-volume, well-specified jobs. Think "write 30 subject line variants from this template".
  • Medium: chat and everyday knowledge work. Think "help me rewrite this paragraph".
  • High: hard research, agentic work and long unattended runs. Think "run this campaign while I'm in a meeting".
  • Xhigh: the hardest long-running agentic work, where you've measured a gain.
  • Max: measuring the ceiling, or the rare task where time and tokens don't matter.

### 03. It finishes (if you tell it to)

The third change is quieter. One early tester quoted on the launch page says [top model] works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint.

The prompting guide is more careful. It says that on long, multistep tasks, [top model] sometimes still ends a turn before the work is done, more often at low and medium effort, and it gives you a block of text to paste that cuts those early stops. That text is in Part 5. It's the single most useful thing in this guide for marketing work, because a campaign is exactly the kind of long, multistep task where a model stops after the plan and asks "want me to continue?"

Part 2: What it built

The launch post opens with demos. They're not marketing demos, but they tell you what kind of job you can now hand over.

### 04. The operating system

One Anthropic engineer gave [top model] the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop: its own core, drivers for the disk, keyboard and network, file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer.

The part that matters to you is not the operating system. It's "coordinated". One model held the plan, split the work, handed it out, checked what came back, and kept going for eight days. That's the shape of a campaign: one plan, many pieces, one person checking the pieces fit.

### 05. Three devices from one paragraph

The second demo: Anthropic asked [top model], in a one-paragraph prompt, to design and produce three working electronic devices, with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures and software. A voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. Anthropic says Claude wrote its own specifications, picked the parts, routed the boards and programmed the devices, each board ready for manufacturing in under a day with minimal human input, and all three worked without electrical changes.

Again, the lesson for a marketer is the brief, not the hardware. One paragraph in. The model wrote its own specifications before doing anything else. That's exactly what you want from a campaign run: you write the brief, it writes the plan, you check the plan.

### 06. What this does not mean

It does not mean [top model] knows your market. It knows what you give it. In the operating system demo, the model had a computer to test its code on. In the device demo, it had a manufacturer building and testing the boards. Every one of those demos had a way to check reality.

Your campaign has no such loop unless you build one. The model does not see your ad account, your analytics, your customers' replies or the live search results. It will write a confident launch plan with targets it can't measure. Part 5 has the fix: every number it can't check gets marked "TO CHECK", and you check it.

Part 3: The campaign

Here's the real run, step by step, so you can copy it.

### 07. The brief

The whole campaign started from one file, brief.md. Here it is, word for word:

# Campaign brief

Product: see input/facts.md. Competitors: input/competitor-surferseo.txt and input/competitor-seranking.txt (their homepage text, captured today).
Audience: owners of small business websites (a plumber, a dentist, a local shop) who know they should "do SEO" and have no time or agency budget.
Goal: more 7-day trials in the next 30 days.
Deliverables, one file each in out/:
1. out/1-competitor-teardown.md: what each competitor promises, to whom, and the gap our audience falls into.
2. out/2-landing-page.md: a landing page for that audience, section by section, with the headline, subhead, 3 benefit blocks, proof we can honestly show, FAQ, CTA.
3. out/3-launch-plan.md: a 30-day launch plan, week by week, channels and one measurable target per week.
4. out/4-email-sequence.md: 5 emails for trial signups (day 0, 1, 3, 5, 7), subject + body, under 120 words each.
Rules: use only the facts in input/. Never invent a customer, a number or a testimonial. Mark anything you could not verify as "TO CHECK".
I approve everything before it ships: nothing is published, sent or bought.

Four things make this brief work, and you should keep all four in yours:

1. The inputs are files, not memory. A facts file about the product, and the text of two competitor homepages captured the same morning. The model never has to remember anything about the product, which means it never has to guess.

2. One audience, described by who they are, not by a persona name. "A plumber, a dentist, a local shop" gives the model a picture. "SMB decision makers" gives it nothing.

3. Every deliverable has a file name and a shape. "3 benefit blocks", "one measurable target per week", "under 120 words each". The review step needs something to check against.

4. The rules say what to do when it doesn't know. "Mark anything you could not verify as TO CHECK" is the line that turns a confident liar into an honest assistant.

### 08. The crew

The folder had four subagent files in `.claude/agents/`, one per deliverable: teardown, landing, launch, emails. Each one is a few lines. The teardown, for example:

---
name: teardown
description: Reads the competitor files and writes out/1-competitor-teardown.md. Use it for that deliverable only.
tools: Read, Write, Glob
---
You are one member of a small marketing crew. Read brief.md and the files in input/ (and out/1-competitor-teardown.md once it exists). Read the competitor files and write out/1-competitor-teardown.md. Use only the facts in input/; never invent a customer, a figure or a testimonial; write "TO CHECK" where you are unsure. Return a 3-line summary of what you wrote.

Notice the tools line. The subagents can read and write files. They cannot browse, cannot send anything, cannot touch anything outside the folder. A crew member with fewer powers makes fewer surprises.

### 09. The one-line task

Then one message to the lead, the main [top model] session, at high effort:

Run the campaign in brief.md. You are the lead: write out/0-plan.md first (who does what, in which order, and what you check before calling it done), then hand each deliverable to its subagent (teardown first, the other three after it, in parallel), then review every file against the brief's rules and fix what breaks them. Finish the whole task: do not stop after the plan.

That's it. No brief per subagent, no step-by-step. The lead writes those.

### 10. The plan it wrote

Before handing out a single job, the lead wrote a plan file. Who does what, in which order, and a checklist it would run before calling the campaign done.

What I didn't expect: the checklist was stricter than my brief. My brief said "never invent a customer, a number or a testimonial". The plan turned that into a list: no customer names, no quotes, no review scores, no user counts, no "X% more traffic", no time savings, no ranking promises. It also said competitor figures could only appear as the competitors' own homepage claims, attributed to them. And it listed, in advance, the gaps it expected to find in the facts file: why a card is asked at signup, what happens when the trial ends, what one credit buys.

This is the "wrote its own specifications" behaviour from the device demo, applied to marketing. And it's the file you should read first in any run, because if the plan is wrong, everything after it is wrong too.

### 11. The teardown

The teardown subagent read the two captured competitor homepages and wrote 2,483 words. Its gap statement, word for word: "Their pages talk to SEO teams. Ours talks to the owner who does it alone."

The part I liked most was a section it wasn't asked for, called "Where we are weaker (say it, do not hide it)". One competitor's page says "No credit card required". The product in my test asks for a card at signup. The teardown said plainly: on this point they win, so say it upfront and don't invent a reason for the card.

The useful part was not the summary of each competitor. It was the gap. Both captured homepages talk to teams: marketing managers, SEO specialists, agencies, enterprises. Neither, in the captured part, names a small business owner. That gap became the angle of the three other files.

### 12. The landing page, the launch plan, the emails

The three other subagents ran at the same time, each reading the teardown first.

The email sequence is the piece I'd ship first. Five emails, bodies of 92, 80, 84, 94 and 95 words, all under the 120 cap. Look at the first one: it says the card thing in the first email, instead of hiding it until day 7. And where it didn't know the link to the signup step, it wrote [LINK TO CHECK] instead of guessing a URL.

The landing page kept every price exactly as the facts file had them, recomputed the yearly saving by hand (6, 10 and 16 euros a month), and left the proof section as "what you can check before you sign up" because the facts file had no customer proof.

The launch plan was the weakest. One target per week, as asked, but week 3 and week 4 targets are written as formulas against a baseline it didn't have ("above B / 4, where B is the number of trial signups in the 28 days before day 1"). Honest, but useless until you fill in B. That's the model telling you it can't see your analytics.

### 13. The review

Here's where it went wrong. The lead started the review: it re-read the four files, recounted the email words by hand ("same five figures"), fixed a clumsy sentence on the landing page, and flagged one more assumption in the emails as TO CHECK. Five fixes in total.

Then it ran out of room. The subagents had written 12,646 words, roughly four times what the brief needed, and the lead kept reading all of it back into its context to review it. The session compacted its memory three times in a row and stopped with an error, before writing its final report. The files were saved. The report never came.

The lesson isn't "the model failed". It's that I didn't cap the length of each file, so the crew wrote long, and the review paid for it. The fix is one line per subagent: a word limit per file. I'll get to that in Part 4.

This is the step that makes the whole thing worth it. A single prompt asking for "a landing page" gets you a landing page. A lead that checks four files against one set of rules gets you four files that tell the same story, with the same prices, the same audience, and no invented proof.

### 14. What it cost and how long it took

Straight from the run's own log: 33 turns, 4 subagents, 14 minutes and 16 seconds, 123,553 output tokens, and $35.88 at API list price. I ran it on a Claude subscription, so that's what it would have cost on the API, not what I paid.

Most of that money went on reading, not writing: the lead and the subagents read the same input files again and again, and the review re-read 12,646 words.

Here's how I'd read that number. It's not "cheap" or "expensive" on its own. Compare it with what the same four files would take you by hand: the teardown, the page, the plan and five emails, all consistent with each other. For most people that's a full day. For an agency, it's a line on an invoice.

Then remember what's not in it: you still read every file. You still settle every TO CHECK. You still decide what ships.

### 15. What I changed before anything shipped

Nothing in this run shipped. That was the rule, and it should be yours. The files are drafts. Every number in the launch plan that the model couldn't measure is marked. Every proof block on the landing page is either a fact from the facts file or an empty slot marked TO CHECK.

Part 4: The money

[top model] is the easiest model to waste money on, because every one of its strengths costs tokens: it thinks before replying, it reads everything you give it, and it happily starts subagents that read everything again.

Here's how to keep the bill sane.

### 16. Pick the effort per job, not per account

The prompting guide is clear on where each level belongs. Medium suits interactive work, chat and everyday knowledge work. High suits hard research, agentic work and long unattended runs, and turns take noticeably longer than at medium.

Mapped to marketing:

  • Low: rewriting 50 product descriptions from a template, tagging 500 customer comments, making 30 subject line variants. Clear task, many items, little judgment.
  • Medium: rewriting one email with you, brainstorming hooks, editing a page together. You're there, you see every reply.
  • High: a campaign run like Part 3. A long, multistep job you'll check at the end, not reply by reply.
  • Xhigh and max: almost never for marketing. If you think you need them, measure first.

The guide also says you can mix levels in one workflow: plan and iterate at medium, then raise the effort for the long, unattended part. That's how I'd work a campaign: write the brief with the model at medium, then launch the run at high.

One more line from the guide worth knowing: at high and above, the model thinks before almost every reply, including a reply to a greeting. If you leave a chat at high and ask quick questions all day, you pay for deep thinking on every one. Drop to medium for the quick stuff.

### 17. Subagents: the planner pattern

Two lines from the guide sit right next to each other, and you need both.

First: early testers had good results with [top model] as the planner and orchestrator for other models. That's the pattern from Part 3. The lead plans and reviews, the subagents do the pieces.

Second: subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs, so check which model your subagents use by default.

That second line is the money line. In Claude Code, a subagent can run on a different, cheaper model than the lead. The planning and the review need [top model]. Writing 5 emails from a clear brief and a clear angle often doesn't. If your teardown and your review are where the judgment is, put [top model] there, and try a cheaper model on the writing subagents. Then compare the files side by side before you decide. Don't take my word for it, and don't take the price list's word for it either.

### 18. When a subagent is worth it

A subagent pays for itself when:

  • The job reads a lot of material the lead doesn't need afterwards. A teardown of 5 competitor sites is the textbook case: the subagent reads them, the lead only gets the conclusions.
  • Several jobs can run at the same time and don't depend on each other. The page, the plan and the emails in Part 3 all depended on the teardown, but not on each other.
  • You want a clean context. A subagent writing emails doesn't need the 3,000 words of the competitor pages in its head.

A subagent is a waste when:

  • The job is small. Starting a crew member to write one headline costs more in reading than the headline costs in writing.
  • The pieces depend on each other line by line. Two subagents writing two halves of one page will contradict each other, and the lead will spend its review fixing it.
  • You have no file to hand over. A subagent briefed from the chat history has to read the chat history.
  • You don't cap its output. My run's crew wrote about four times what the brief needed, and the lead's review choked on it. Give every subagent a word limit per file.

The guide adds a nuance: if your prompts or agent files tell the model to delegate, it delegates readily. If they don't, it rarely starts a subagent on short tasks. So the old habit of writing "always use subagents" in your setup is now a cost line, not a speed trick. Name the jobs that deserve a subagent, and only those.

### 19. Where [top model] is a waste

I'll be blunt about it, since nobody else will:

  • A single social post. Use the model you're already using.
  • Bulk rewriting with a fixed template. Low effort, or a cheaper model.
  • Anything you'll redo by hand anyway. If you always rewrite the AI's headlines, stop asking the most expensive model for them.
  • A campaign with no facts file. [top model] at high effort will produce something very convincing out of nothing. That's worse, not better.

### 20. The rule of thumb

[top model] for the plan and the review. Effort set per job. A word limit on every file. Subagents only for jobs that read a lot or run in parallel. Cheaper models for the volume. And a file of facts, always.

Part 5: Use it

Here's everything you need to run your own campaign this afternoon.

### 21. The finishing text

This block comes straight from Anthropic's prompting guide, in the section called "Finish the whole task". The guide says [top model] sometimes ends a turn before the work is done on long, multistep tasks, and suggests adding text like this to your system prompt:

# Finishing work
Please avoid stopping while you still owe work the user asked for. Be persistent and do not stop unless needed.

While status notes are welcome, as is clarifying with the user on open decisions, carry on with work that does not depend on the user's answer without unnecessary stops.

If you notice yourself inviting the user to redirect you or offering to wait, instead proceed on the next part of the task. You may meet ordinary obstacles like errors, timeouts, locked files, empty results or failing tools. Diagnose them first, and when they are not real blockers, work through them with the access you have (wait and retry, fix the request, use another tool or source) rather than stopping unnecessarily.

If someone clearly decided something is a hard blocker, such as a file marked not to be touched, access that was intentionally withheld, or a safety guardrail, leave it alone, say plainly what you found, and look for another safe way to finish the task. Stopping before the task is complete is very rarely merited, as in when the task can't move forward without user input, or where the blocker is deliberate and should not be worked past. This does not override the need for confirmation on risky or destructive actions.

In my run, I didn't use the full block. I wrote one short line in the task instead ("Finish the whole task: do not stop after the plan") and ran at high effort, where early stops are rarer. If you run at medium, paste the whole block. The guide says that in Anthropic's own replay at medium effort, a version of this text cut the sessions that ended with doable work left by about half, and raised output tokens by about 30 percent. So it costs something. It's worth it for a campaign.

### 22. The setup, in five minutes

1. Make a folder for the campaign. Inside it: `brief.md`, an `input/` folder, an `out/` folder, and `.claude/agents/`.

2. In `input/`, put a facts file about your product (what it is, who it's for, prices, the offer, what you can prove) and the text of 2 or 3 competitor pages. Copy and paste is fine. Date the capture.

3. Write the brief with the four rules from step 07: files not memory, one audience, every deliverable with a name and a shape, and the TO CHECK rule.

4. Add one subagent file per deliverable, with read and write tools only, and a word limit for its file (my run skipped this and paid for it).

5. Open Claude Code in the folder, set [top model] at high effort, and send the one-line task from step 09.

Then go do something else. Come back to `out/0-plan.md` first.

### 23. Prompt: the facts file

You don't have a facts file? Make one with the model, then check every line yourself:

I am going to paste the text of my homepage and my pricing page.
Turn them into a facts file for a marketing campaign, as a bullet list:
- what the product is, in one sentence
- who it is for
- what it does (features as the page states them)
- prices and plans, exactly as written
- the offer (trial, guarantee, signup conditions)
- every proof the page shows (numbers, logos, reviews), quoted word for word
Use only what is on the pages. If something a marketer would need is missing (a price, a trial condition, a proof), write it as "MISSING: <what>".
Date the file with today's date.

### 24. Prompt: the competitor teardown

Read the competitor files in input/ and write out/1-competitor-teardown.md.
For each competitor: the promise (quote their headline and subhead word for word), who they say it is for (quote their own words), and the proof they show (marked "their claim, not verified").
Then one section: the gap. Which part of my audience, described in brief.md, does none of them speak to, and what words would that audience use that none of them uses?
Use only the files. If a capture is cut off, say where it stops and do not guess what comes after.

### 25. Prompt: the landing page

Using brief.md, input/facts.md and out/1-competitor-teardown.md, write out/2-landing-page.md for the audience in the brief.
Sections, in this order: headline, subhead, 3 benefit blocks (each one a benefit in the audience's words, then the fact from facts.md that backs it), a proof section, an FAQ of 5 questions, a CTA.
Proof: only what facts.md lets us show. Where proof is missing, leave an empty slot marked "TO CHECK: <what proof would go here>". Never invent a customer, a number or a quote.
Write like you're talking to the owner of a small shop: plain words, short sentences, no jargon.

### 26. Prompt: the launch plan and the emails

Using the same files, write two drafts.
1. out/3-launch-plan.md: a 30-day plan, week by week. For each week: the channel, the actions, and ONE measurable target. If you don't know the current baseline for a target, write "TO CHECK: baseline" next to it. Mark every action that costs money as "DECISION: spend".
2. out/4-email-sequence.md: 5 emails for people who just started a trial (day 0, 1, 3, 5, 7). Subject + body, under 120 words each. Each email does one job (welcome, first result, a common blocker, proof, the end of the trial). Only facts from facts.md.
Count the words of each email body and fix any that go over.

### 27. Prompt: the review

If you don't run a lead with subagents, run this at the end of any session where you produced several pieces:

Review every file in out/ against brief.md and input/facts.md.
1. List every price, number, claim and proof in the files. For each one: the line in facts.md that backs it, or "NOT IN FACTS".
2. Fix every "NOT IN FACTS" item: remove it, or mark it "TO CHECK".
3. Check the files tell the same story: same audience, same offer wording, same prices.
4. Check each deliverable's shape against the brief (number of blocks, word limits, one target per week).
Fix what breaks the rules directly in the files, then give me the list of open TO CHECK items I must settle before anything ships.

What I'd change in the brief next time

One run teaches you more than ten articles about a model, so here's what I'd change before running it again. None of it is clever. All of it comes from reading the five files and the log.

First, a word limit on every file. The brief said "under 120 words" for the emails, and the emails respected it. It said nothing about the length of the teardown, the page or the plan, so each subagent wrote between 2,400 and 4,500 words, with notes for the reviewer on almost every block. Those notes were useful. But the lead had to read all of them back, and that's what broke the review. Next time: teardown under 800 words, landing page under 900, launch plan under 1,000, and every note for review in one list at the end of the file instead of under each block.

Second, a baseline file. The launch plan couldn't set a real target for weeks 3 and 4 because it didn't know how many trials the product gets today. That's not the model's fault. It's one number, and I didn't give it. Next time, `input/baseline.md` with last month's trials, visits to the pricing page, and the signups by channel, even if they're rough.

Third, a review that doesn't need to hold everything at once. Instead of the lead re-reading four long files in one go, ask it to review one file at a time and write its findings to `out/5-review.md` after each one. If the session runs out of room, the findings are already saved.

Fourth, decide the open questions before the run, not after. The facts file didn't say why a card is asked at signup or what happens when the trial ends, so all four files carry the same TO CHECK about it. Two lines in the facts file would have removed dozens of those marks.

Fifth, keep the "never invent" rule exactly as it is. It's the line that made the run worth reading. Every gap the model hit became a mark you can check, not a confident sentence you'd have to catch.

What [top model] can't see alone

This is the honest-limits section, and it matters more than the prompts.

[top model] sees what's in the folder. It doesn't see:

  • Your ad account. It can't tell you which ad is working.
  • Your analytics. It can't tell you where your trials come from.
  • The live market. It doesn't know what your competitors changed this week unless you paste it.
  • Search data. It doesn't know how many people search what, or who ranks where.

Every one of those is something you plug in as a file, or through a tool that has the data. In my test, the competitor pages were pasted by hand that morning. For search data specifically, a tool connected to live search results and Search Console is what fills the gap. That's what the product in my test does, and the reason I work with the team behind it.

What this does not prove

To be straight with you:

  • One run. Not ten, not a hundred. Another run on the same brief will produce different files. Run yours twice and compare before you trust any one of them.
  • One product, one audience. A campaign for a B2B tool with a sales team behind it is a different job.
  • Drafts, not results. Nothing in this run shipped, so I can't tell you how many trials it brings. Anyone who tells you a model's campaign "converted" after one morning is guessing.
  • The benchmark numbers in Part 1 are Anthropic's, from coding evaluations. They tell you how the effort setting behaves, not how good the copy is.
  • The token numbers in step 14 are from this one run. A brief with ten competitor pages costs more.

What I would do this week

1. Write a facts file for your product. Thirty minutes, by hand or with the prompt in step 23. You'll reuse it for every campaign.

2. Capture the text of your 3 closest competitors' homepages. Date it.

3. Run the campaign from Part 3 once, at high effort, with the finishing text.

4. Read the plan first, then every file. Settle every TO CHECK.

5. Ship one piece. Just one. The email sequence is usually the easiest to test.

6. Next week, run it again with what you learned in the brief.

Before you ask

Do I need Claude Code, or does the Claude app work?

The app works for single pieces. For the crew in Part 3 (a lead, subagents, a folder of files), Claude Code is the simplest place to run it today.

Can I use this for paid ads?

For the teardown and the copy, yes. For deciding the budget, no: the model doesn't see your ad account. Mark every spend as a decision, like the brief in Part 3 does.

Will it make things up?

It can, especially at high effort with no facts. That's why the brief has the TO CHECK rule and the lead has a review step. In my run, the files carry 184 lines marked TO CHECK instead of guesses. Check yours anyway.

Is high effort always better?

No. High is for the long, unattended run. For a chat where you're editing together, medium is faster and cheaper, and the guide says so too.

What about Mythos 5.2?

Anthropic says it's the same underlying model. For marketing work, [top model] is the one you'll actually have.

Final Thoughts

The headline demos are about an operating system and three devices. The lesson for marketers is smaller and more useful: one brief, a plan the model writes itself, a crew that does the pieces, and a review against your rules. That's a campaign.

The model is new. The discipline isn't: facts in, drafts out, you decide what ships.
